title: Science Fiction
objective: After this level you can explain why science fiction films use imagined futures and visitors to talk about fears of their own time.
summary: 1950s science fiction carried atomic-age fears: a visitor warns Earth about its bombs, bomb tests breed giant ants, and pod people have been read as Cold War allegory.

cards.headline: In 1951, a flying saucer landed in Washington with a warning.
cards.body: In The Day the Earth Stood Still, directed by Robert Wise, a visitor named Klaatu arrives and warns that humanity's atomic weapons threaten other civilizations. Britannica calls it a classic that reflects the fears of the Cold War and the early atomic age. The spaceship was imaginary. The worry was not.

cards.headline: Giant ants from a real test site
cards.body: Level 7's A Trip to the Moon was fantasy made with camera tricks such as stop motion and superimposition. By the 1950s, science fiction's monsters had a return address. In Them! (1954), giant ants mutated by atomic bomb tests in the New Mexico desert threaten humanity. Britannica calls it arguably the best of the decade's giant atomic-mutant creature movies. The fear was real; the film just gave it six legs.

cards.headline: Your neighbor, but not quite
cards.body: In Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956), directed by Don Siegel, aliens grow in seedpods and take over people's bodies while they sleep, leaving copies with no human emotion. Made at the height of the Cold War, it has been read as a picture of Cold War paranoia, fear of McCarthyism, the alienation of mass society, or life under communism. Siegel said he intended no political message. Each audience found its own fear in the pods.

cards.headline: Science fiction: decoded
learned: Science fiction turns real fears into imagined threats
The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951): a warning about atomic weapons
Them! (1954): giant ants from atomic bomb tests
Body Snatchers (1956): pod people read as Cold War fears

questions.prompt: In The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951), the visitor Klaatu warns Earth about _____.

options.label: a coming ice age
options.rationale: His warning is about weapons, not weather.

options.label: seedpods that copy sleepers
options.rationale: That's Invasion of the Body Snatchers.

questions.explanation: Klaatu warns that humanity's atomic weapons threaten other civilizations.

questions.prompt: Why have critics read Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956) as a Cold War film, even though Siegel said he intended no political message?

options.label: Its emotionless copies fit the era's fears
Siegel announced that it was about communism
options.rationale: He said he intended no political message.

options.label: It shows an atomic bomb test on screen
options.rationale: That's where Them!'s ants come from.

options.label: It was made by a Soviet film studio
options.rationale: Nothing on the level says so; it is an American film.

questions.explanation: Made at the height of the Cold War, its pod people have been read as an allegory of paranoia, McCarthyism, mass-society alienation or communism.

questions.prompt: Level 7's A Trip to the Moon made fantasy with stop motion and superimposition. What did 1950s films like Them! add to their monsters?

options.label: Camera tricks such as superimposition
options.rationale: Méliès was already using those in 1902.

options.label: A story loosely based on Jules Verne
The first trip into space on film
options.rationale: Méliès's spacecraft reached the Moon in 1902.

options.label: A link to a real fear: atomic bomb tests

questions.explanation: Them!'s giant ants were mutated by atomic bomb tests, tying the fantasy to a real fear of the 1950s.
